1 Introduction

1.1 Business context

I am an entry-level analyst at an investment firm that finances sustainable infrastructure and applies responsible-investment principles. My line manager asked for four pieces of work:

  1. Most common climate hazards affecting communities globally
  2. Number of planned projects and total funding sought, by region
  3. Ranked list of collaboration / investment opportunities
  4. Best model to predict environmental controversy involvement, with evaluation

Findings: 1. env_projects.csv has 2590 rows (one row = one planned project) and 26 columns;

  1. env_controversy.csv has 7275 firms (one row per firm) and 26 columns.

  2. Both datasets haven’t appropriate data type which may affect the analysis. So, before analysing, we have to change the existing data type to their respective appropriate data type.

2.4 Duplicate Data Checking

Duplicate rows would be counted twice, and missing values can bias totals or break models. I therefore check both datasets for duplicates, missing values and impossible values before any analysis, and I record each decision so the work can be replicated.

duplicated() flags rows that are identical in every column. I also look for “near duplicates” (the same city and the same project description appearing more than once), which would suggest double entry.

Findings: There are 4 exact duplicate rows (each of these four cities, Busan, Gwangju, Chapel Hill and Sanggau, appears twice with every field identical and no project details). I removed them, so the working table has 2586 rows (from 2590).

There is no duplicate rows in firms data.

2.5 Missing Value Checking

Interpretation: missingness is heavy in the collaboration flags (collab_business is missing for about 63% of rows), in project costs, and in firm emissions (env_co2s3 is missing for about half of firms). Missing collaboration flags are probably “not reported” rather than “No”, so I treat only collab_business == 1 as confirmed experience. In the firm data, missing emissions mostly means the firm does not disclose them, so later I will keep a “was missing” indicator when I build the model. There are a few exact duplicate project rows, which I remove.

2.6 Cleaning the project data

Steps and reasons:

  1. distinct() removes exact duplicate rows so projects are not double counted.
  2. The text columns contain leftover escape codes such as \n and \uXXXX from the raw survey export, so I write a small cleaning function with stringr and stringi.
  3. The project description starts with a project type (for example “Transport - …”), so I extract it with a regular expression. This is data extraction from text.

The climate hazard text and the economic indicators are repeated on every project row of a city. I check that each city has exactly one value so that I can safely collapse to one row per city.

3 Part 1: Most common climate hazards affecting communities

The column climate_hazard is free text. For each city it contains several hazards written like Hazard name: description | Hazard name: description .... To answer “which hazards are most common”, I need to extract the hazard names from the text and then count how many cities report each hazard. Then I look at the descriptions with text analysis to see how communities are affected, I test whether differences between regions are statistically real, and finally I use PCA and clustering to see whether groups of similar cities face different hazards.

3.1 City profile

Interpretation: the data are global but not evenly spread. North America, Latin America, Europe and “UKWW” (the label used in the dataset, mostly UK, South Africa and Türkiye) dominate, while India, Japan and China have only a handful of cities each. So conclusions about those three regions will be weak. The United States, Brazil and the United Kingdom supply the largest number of cities. I used a log scale for population because city size is very right-skewed.

3.2 Extracting the hazard names from the text

My steps:

  1. Split each city’s text on the separator |.
  2. Keep the words before the first colon as the hazard name.
  3. A few descriptions themselves contain | or colons, which would create false “hazard names”. To avoid this I keep only names that appear in the official list of hazards used in the survey. I build the list from names that occur often (at least 4 cities) and are short.
  4. Merge spelling variants (for example “urban flooding” and “Urban flooding”).
## Number of hazard types found: 24
## City-hazard records: 3294 from 675 cities

I also group the detailed hazards into broader families. I do this because some hazards describe the same real-world problem (for example heat stress and extreme heat), and managers think in families.

## character(0)

3.3 The most common hazards

I count the percentage of cities that report each hazard. I use percentages of cities (684) rather than raw project counts because a city is the unit that experiences a hazard.

Top 10 hazards by number of cities reporting them
Hazard Family Cities % of cities
Extreme heat Heat 447 66.2%
Urban flooding Flooding and heavy rain 380 56.3%
Drought Drought and water scarcity 317 47.0%
Heavy precipitation Flooding and heavy rain 266 39.4%
River flooding Flooding and heavy rain 217 32.1%
Fire weather (risk of wildfires) Wildfire 208 30.8%
Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise) Flooding and heavy rain 174 25.8%
Storm Storms and wind 143 21.2%
Other Other 124 18.4%
Extreme wind Storms and wind 123 18.2%

Findings: the top three individual hazards are extreme heat, urban flooding and drought. When I group hazards into families, flooding and heavy rain is the broadest problem (about nine in ten cities mention at least one flood-type hazard), followed by heat (about three in four cities) and drought / water scarcity (a little over half). This tells me that the climate risks to communities are mainly about too much water, too little water and too much heat. These are the threats that infrastructure such as drainage, wastewater, waste and water systems, and cooling or green space projects must address.

3.4 How many hazards does a city report?

Findings: A typical city reports about five hazards, so risks are compound. For investors this means a single project (for example nature-based flood protection) can have several benefits.

3.5 Hazards by region

Findings: The heatmap shows that hazards are not equally common everywhere. Extreme heat is reported by roughly 80% of North American and UKWW cities and about 73% of European cities, but only about one third of cities in South East Asia & Oceania. Urban flooding and drought are reported fairly evenly across the big regions (about 50-60% of cities), while fire weather is mostly a North American, European and Latin American concern (around 40% of cities) and is almost absent from the Asian regions. Regions with very few cities (China, India, Japan) should not be over-interpreted. In 1.6 I test statistically whether these regional differences are real.

3.6 Text analysis of the hazard descriptions (how are communities affected?)

Counting names only tells which hazards occur. The descriptions tell who and what is affected. I use text-analysis tools from class.

3.6.1 Pre-processing and term frequency

Computers cannot read sentences, so I convert the text to a “tidy” table with one word per row (unnest_tokens), remove very common words (stop_words), and also remove survey words that appear everywhere but carry no meaning (for example “city” or “climate”). Then I count words.

## Number of word tokens after cleaning: 206255

Findings: the most frequent words relate to water, heat, health, flooding, vulnerable groups and infrastructure. This agrees with the hazard counts. Words such as “health”, “vulnerable”, “low” and “income” show that the descriptions repeatedly talk about vulnerable people, especially low-income households, which is the social side of the risk.

3.6.2 Word pairs (bigrams)

Findings: Phrases give more context than single words. The most frequent pairs are “low income”, “extreme heat”, “vulnerable populations”, “water supply”, “heat waves” and “sea level” (rise). They show the mechanisms (heat waves, sea level rise, air quality) and the groups at risk (low-income households, outdoor workers), which helps connect hazards with infrastructure solutions.

3.6.3 Three Words (trigrams)

Findings: The top 6 most frequent three words are “low income households”, “sea level rise”, “extreme weather events”, “poor air quality”, “heat related illness” and “urban heat island. They also show the mechanisms (heat waves, sea level rise, air quality) and the groups at risk (low-income households, outdoor workers), which helps connect hazards with infrastructure solutions.

3.6.4 Four Words (quadgrams)

Findings: The phrases contain income and heat in most frequently. It is apparent that the context squeezes if we increase number of words and sample size also decreases. Thus, in our case, its better to use bigram to understand the hazard descriptions efficiently.

3.6.5 Which words are special to each hazard family? (TF-IDF)

Plain word counts are dominated by common words. TF-IDF gives a high score to words that are frequent in one group but rare in the others, so it highlights what is distinctive.

Findings: The distinctive words make sense: wildfire descriptions focus on smoke and fire, flooding on rain and drainage, drought on water supply and agriculture, and cold hazards on snow and ice. This is a good sanity check that my hazard extraction worked.

3.6.6 Sentiment of the descriptions

I use the bing lexicon (positive vs negative words). Climate hazard descriptions are expected to be mostly negative; I want to see which hazards sound the most negative.

Findings: Every family has a clearly negative net score (roughly -0.5 to -0.7), as expected for descriptions of damage and vulnerability. Wildfire and flooding descriptions are the most negative, while heat and health are slightly less negative, possibly because those descriptions also mention support programmes and protective actions. A limitation I should mention: lexicon methods count words only and do not understand context (for example “protect” is positive even when talking about a risk).

3.6.7 Topic modelling (LDA)

To check what themes exist without telling the model the hazard names, I use Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). I combine all descriptions for each city into one document, build a document-term matrix, and ask for 4 topics. The number of topics is a judgement call; 4 gives themes that are easy to interpret.

Findings: LDA does not name its topics, so I read the top words of each topic and name the themes myself. In my run the topics separate into themes that line up with the hazard families (for example heat and health of vulnerable people, rain / flooding and drainage damage, water supply and drought, and storms or coastal damage to infrastructure).

3.7 Statistical inference and bivariate analysis

So far I have only described the sample. Here I ask whether the patterns are statistically significant. I use three tests and I check assumptions where relevant.

3.7.1 Confidence intervals for the share of cities reporting each hazard family

family cities share 95% CI
Heat 506 75.0% 71.5% to 78.2%
Flooding / heavy rain 607 89.9% 87.3% to 92.0%
Drought / water scarcity 379 56.1% 52.3% to 59.9%

Findings: The intervals are narrow because the sample has several hundred cities, so I can be fairly confident about how widespread each hazard family is among the cities in the CDP / ICLEI sample. (A caveat: these cities chose to report, so they may not represent all communities worldwide.)

3.7.2 Is extreme heat reporting related to region? (chi-squared test)

Both variables are categorical, so I use a chi-squared test of independence. Some regions have very few cities, so expected counts are small. To be safe I use a simulated p-value.

##                            
##                             FALSE TRUE
##   China                         3    2
##   Europe                       10   92
##   India                         2   12
##   Japan                         4   14
##   Latin America                50   97
##   North America                16  161
##   South East Asia & Oceania    74   47
##   UKWW                         10   81
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test with simulated p-value (based on 5000
##  replicates)
## 
## data:  tab_heat
## X-squared = 140.93, df = NA, p-value = 2e-04

Findings: The null hypothesis is that heat reporting is independent of region. The simulated p-value is 2e-04, which is far below 0.05, so I reject the null and conclude that heat reporting rates really differ across regions (very high in North America, Europe and UKWW, much lower in South East Asia & Oceania and China). This matters for investors because it suggests that regional strategies (not one global strategy) are needed. One caution: reporting rates may also reflect how thoroughly a city completed the survey, not only the true hazard.

3.7.3 Do cities reporting drought differ in water services? (t-test and Wilcoxon test)

Hypothesis: cities in countries with less safely managed drinking water may be more likely to report drought or water stress.

** I compare soc_water for cities that report a drought-family hazard against those that do not.

## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  soc_water by drought
## t = -0.47971, df = 559.89, p-value = 0.6316
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group FALSE and group TRUE is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -4.361335  2.649177
## sample estimates:
## mean in group FALSE  mean in group TRUE 
##            85.42074            86.27682
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  soc_water by drought
## W = 42655, p-value = 0.3337
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

Findings: safe-water coverage is strongly left-skewed (many countries are near 100%), so the t-test assumption of normality is doubtful. That is why I also run the Wilcoxon test as a robustness check. Both tests give the same answer: the Welch t-test p-value is 0.63 and the Wilcoxon p-value is 0.33, and the two group means are very close (about 85.4% vs 86.3%). So my hypothesis was not supported: there is no evidence that cities reporting drought sit in countries with weaker water services. Drought and water scarcity affect cities in both well-served and poorly-served countries. For an investor this is a useful finding: water-resilience projects are relevant everywhere, not only in developing countries.

India-Europe -2.597 -4.818 -0.375 0.010 
## 
##  Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test
## 
## data:  n_haz by cityregion
## Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 81.083, df = 7, p-value = 8.281e-15

Findings: ANOVA tests whether at least one region has a different average number of hazards, and Tukey’s test shows which pairs differ. The ANOVA p-value is extremely small, so the average number of hazards clearly differs between regions. North America, UKWW and Europe report the most hazards per city (roughly 5.4 to 5.6) while South East Asia & Oceania, Japan, China and India report fewer (roughly 2.8 to 3.6). Hazard counts are small integers and not normally distributed, so I confirm the result with the Kruskal-Wallis test, which agrees. The gap may partly reflect different reporting practices, not only different climate exposure.

3.7.5 Correlation between city indicators

Findings: National GDP and greenhouse gas emissions are very strongly correlated (about 0.9), which simply says that big economies emit more in total. R&D spending is strongly correlated with sanitation (about 0.77) and safe water (about 0.65), and safe water and sanitation are correlated with each other (about 0.69), so they all describe the national level of development. GDP growth is negatively correlated with safe water (about -0.5), which is typical of fast-growing emerging economies that still have service gaps. Highly correlated variables carry overlapping information, which is exactly why I use PCA next.

3.8 PCA and cluster analysis of cities

The city and country indicators are many and correlated. PCA compresses them into a few uncorrelated components, and clustering then groups cities with a similar socio-economic profile. I then check whether the clusters face different hazards.

I use log transforms for skewed variables, replace missing values with the median, scale all variables, and run prcomp().

Variance explained by the first five components
PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4 PC5
Standard deviation 1.663 1.327 1.211 1.002 0.981
Proportion of Variance 0.276 0.176 0.147 0.100 0.096
Cumulative Proportion 0.276 0.453 0.599 0.700 0.796

Findings: The scree plot shows that no single component dominates: the first component explains roughly 28% of the variance, the first four about 70% and the first five about 80%. This tells me the indicators describe several different dimensions rather than one. In the variable plot, variables pointing in the same direction are positively correlated. The first component is mostly driven by national economic size and development (GDP, R&D spending, emissions and sanitation), so it separates large, more developed economies from the rest. The later components mix growth, unemployment, inflation and export dependence.

3.8.1 K-means clustering

I choose the number of clusters using the elbow and silhouette methods, then fit k-means on the first components.

Cluster profiles
cluster cities median_pop median_gdp_bn mean_water mean_inflation top_region
1 200 165613 530.8 95.5 3.0 Europe

Findings: The three clusters differ mainly in economic size, water services and inflation. In my run one cluster is dominated by Latin American cities in emerging economies with the weakest safe-water coverage (about two thirds of the population) and the highest inflation; one is mostly European cities in smaller, high-service economies; and one is mostly North American cities in the largest economy. Flooding is reported by more than 80% of cities in every cluster, and drought is similarly common in all three (roughly 53% to 59%), which again shows that these are global problems and not limited to one type of economy. The emerging-economy cluster reports relatively more health and land-related hazards (such as landslides) but less heat, cold and wildfire than the other two.

3.9 Summary of main findings for Part 1

  1. Most common hazards. Out of 675 cities, the three most reported single hazards are Extreme heat (66%), Urban flooding (56%) and Drought (47%).

  2. By family, Flooding and heavy rain is the broadest problem (90% of cities), followed by heat and drought / water scarcity. The main climate risks are therefore too much water, too little water and too much heat.

  3. Compound risk. The average city reports about 4.9 hazards, so projects that address several hazards at once (nature-based solutions, resilient water and waste systems) are attractive.

  4. Who is affected. Text analysis shows that the descriptions focus on health, vulnerable and low-income households, outdoor workers, water supply and infrastructure damage. Sentiment is negative for every hazard family, and the LDA topics broadly match the hazard families.

  5. Regional differences are real, national water services are not the driver of drought. The chi-squared, ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests show that heat reporting and the number of hazards differ by region, so investment strategy should be adapted by region. In contrast, the t-test and Wilcoxon test found no link between drought reporting and national safe-water coverage.

  6. Limitations. The data are self-reported by cities that chose to disclose, regions such as India, Japan and China have very few cities, and hazard names were extracted from free text.

4 Part 2: Planned projects and funding sought by region

My manager wants the total number of planned projects and the total value of funding sought for each region. The columns I use are:

  • a project = one row of the project table that has at least some project information (rows where every project field is empty are cities that did not list a project, so I do not count them),

  • funding sought = project_investmentcost (the “total investment cost needed”), because this is the amount a financier would be asked to provide. project_totalcost is the overall project cost and may include money that is already secured.

4.1 Checking the cost data before summing

Before adding up money, I always check for outliers, because a single data-entry error can ruin a total. I look at the largest values.

My cleaning rule is: an investment cost larger than the national GDP is treated as an error and excluded from totals (the project is still counted as a planned project). 5 Part 3: Ranked list of collaboration and investment opportunities

5.1 Turning the scenario into selection rules

The scenario gives me four business criteria. I translate each into a filter in R:

  1. Industry expertise in waste management: Project type starts with “Waste management” or the description contains waste-related words (waste, recycling, landfill, compost, circular economy and similar). I exclude wastewater (which is a water-sector project) and “waste heat” (an energy project).

  2. Prefers partners who have collaborated with private for-profit organisations: collab_business == 1 (confirmed past collaboration). Missing values are not treated as “yes”.

  3. Track record of loans and public-private partnerships: for public sector projects project_fundingmodel contains “Loans” (commercial banks or international financial institutions) or “Public-private partnership”.

  4. Needs a known investment cost to rank: project_investmentcost is available, above zero and not flagged as an error.

Then I rank the surviving projects in descending order of investment cost sought, as my manager asked.

5.2 Applying the filters

Findings: The funnel shows that the firm’s criteria are quite selective. Waste projects are common, but only a minority come from cities with confirmed private-sector collaboration and a loan or PPP funding model, and fewer still have a reported investment cost. In my run the funnel goes from 2,477 projects to 438 waste projects, 140 with business collaboration, 51 with a loan or PPP funding model and finally 31 with a usable cost. Because of this, the final list is short and highly targeted, which suits an investment firm that wants a manageable pipeline.

5.5 Supporting analysis: what drives project investment cost? (linear regression)

The ranking is by cost, so I want to understand what makes projects expensive. Cost is extremely right-skewed, so I model the log (base 10) of the investment cost. That way a coefficient can be read as a multiplication of cost. I use cleaned positive costs from all projects (not only waste projects) to have enough data.

Findings: The log-log relationship between population and cost is positive, so larger cities plan bigger projects. In the regression, each coefficient shows how many “powers of ten” the cost changes when the variable increases by one unit while the others are held fixed; the cost multiplier column converts this into a plain multiple (for example 2 means about twice the cost). In my output, population and national GDP both have positive, highly significant effects (a ten-times larger city is associated with roughly 3 times higher project cost, since 10^0.5 is about 3.2). Compared with Europe (the reference region), projects in India and Latin America are much cheaper (about 5% and 15% of the European cost, holding other things equal), transport projects are about four times more expensive than the “other types” group, and cities with confirmed business collaboration plan projects roughly 2.4 times larger. Waste management projects are not significantly more or less expensive than the reference group. The R-squared is modest (about 0.18), which tells me that city size, national income, region and project type explain only part of the variation in project cost; much of the cost depends on the specific project. The diagnostic plots are reasonably acceptable after the log transformation: there is no strong funnel shape in the residuals, and the Q-Q plot follows the line apart from some tail departures. I therefore use this model to describe what is associated with cost and not to predict costs of single projects. Note that the regression shows association and not causation.

6 Part 4: Predicting environmental controversy risk

6.1 Understanding the business problem

Ultimate goal is to build a classification model that predicts whether a firm is involved in an environmental controversy (env_contro = Yes). The model is for initial screening: firms flagged as high risk will be reviewed by experts.

Judgement:

  • Only about 2.8% of firms are positives, so a model that says “No controversy” for everybody would be 97% accurate and completely useless. Accuracy is therefore not a good metric here.

  • The scenario says false positives are relatively cheap but false negatives are costly (a risky firm slips through). So I care most about sensitivity (recall): the share of truly controversial firms that we catch.

  • I will still watch precision and the share of firms flagged, because experts have limited time.

  • To compare models fairly without choosing a threshold I use ROC AUC and PR AUC (area under the precision-recall curve; this is more informative than ROC AUC when positives are rare). Then I choose the final decision threshold separately, using the F2 score, which weights recall more heavily than precision.

6.2 Data preparation

6.2.1 Feature engineering and the train / test split

Steps followed:

  1. Create ratio features. Raw emissions, energy and capital expenditure mostly reflect firm size. Dividing by revenue or assets (intensity) tells me whether the firm is inefficient for its size.

  2. Split the data first into a training set (75%) and a test set (25%), stratified by the outcome so both sets keep about 2.8% positives. The test set stays untouched until the very end, to give an honest estimate of performance on new firms.

  3. Learn all pre-processing rules (medians, transformations, scaling) from the training set only, then apply the same rules to the test set, so no information from the test set leaks into the model.

I build the whole machine-learning workflow with base R and a few classic packages (rpart, glmnet, pROC, class). This is a transparent way to see exactly what happens in each step, and it needs no extra modelling framework.

Both sets keep the same share of controversial firms (stratified split)
set firms controversies share
Training 5456 154 2.82%
Test 1819 52 2.86%

Findings: the stratified split keeps the same class balance in both sets. The test set has only about 50 controversial firms, so test results will be noisy and I will report an uncertainty range later.

6.2.2 Pre-processing rules

  1. Missing-value indicators: Missing emissions or cost data often means “not disclosed”, which could itself be a signal

  2. Median imputation: Logistic regression and KNN cannot handle missing values. The median is robust to outliers.

  3. Yeo-Johnson transformation: Financial and emission variables are extremely right-skewed, and some (ROE, revenue) contain negative values, so a log transform would fail. Yeo-Johnson handles negatives. I estimate its parameter (lambda) by maximum likelihood.

  4. Standardisation (mean 0, sd 1): KNN uses distances, and PCA and penalised regression work better when variables are on the same scale.

5.Lump rare categories: Industry has 59 levels and headquarters country has 63; I keep categories with at least 1% of training firms and group the rest as “other”.

  1. Dummy variables: Models need numbers, not text categories.

  2. Drop zero-variance columns: A column that never changes carries no information.

I write the pre-processing as two functions: learn_prep() learns the rules from a data set, and apply_prep() applies them to any data.

I explore only the training data so that the test set stays unseen.

Findings: about 97% of firms have no controversy. Any model must handle this imbalance, otherwise it will simply predict “No” for everyone.

6.3.1 Industry and country

Findings: controversy rates are clearly higher in resource-heavy industries (oil and gas and related services are far above average) and in some countries. This is a strong sign that industry and country carry predictive information, which is why I keep them (grouped) in the model.

Findings: I use the Wilcoxon test because these variables are very skewed and have outliers. Variables with small p-values (typically firm size measures such as market capitalisation, assets and revenue, and emissions) differ significantly between the two groups: controversial firms tend to be bigger and higher-emitting. The Welch t-test on log market capitalisation confirms the size difference. Remember that statistical significance only tells me a difference exists, not that it is large enough to predict well on its own.

6.3.3 Policies and controversy

Findings: The direction may look counter-intuitive: firms that have environmental policies show a higher controversy rate. I think this is not because policies cause controversies. Instead, large firms are more likely to both publish policies and attract media attention.

Chi-squared tests show which differences are statistically significant: in my output every policy difference is significant at the 5% level except the share of green products. This is an important reminder that the model finds associations, so it should be used for screening and not for blaming firms.

6.3.4 Missing data as a signal and correlations

Findings: firms that report emissions data are more often involved in controversies than firms that do not report (probably because reporting firms are larger and more visible). The correlation plot shows strong correlations among the size variables (assets, revenue, costs, market capitalisation, capex) and among the emission variables. This multicollinearity can make logistic regression coefficients unstable, and it is a good reason to try PCA.

6.4 Dimensionality reduction (PCA) and cluster analysis

6.4.1 PCA on the numeric predictors:

Many predictors are correlated. PCA replaces them with a smaller number of uncorrelated components. I run it on the pre-processed training data (already transformed and standardised).

Cumulative variance explained

Findings: the first components capture the size and emissions dimension (PC1) and the profitability / leverage dimension (later components). The scatter plot shows that the two groups overlap heavily: controversial firms are not separated cleanly from the others. This warns me that the prediction task is hard and that I should not expect a near-perfect model. I will use PCA as an alternative pre-processing choice for logistic regression in 4.6.

6.4.2 Cluster analysis (k-means) of firms

Clustering is unsupervised, so it does not use the outcome. If some clusters of similar firms have a much higher controversy rate, this tells me there are firm “types” that carry more environmental risk.

I pick the number of clusters with the silhouette method (on a sample of firms, because silhouette needs all pairwise distances).

Profile of the firm clusters
cluster firms controversy_rate median_marketcap_m median_env_score share_climate_policy
1 1,975 1.6% 282.9 24.9 42%
2 830 8.0% 9,455.5 72.8 80%
3 2,651 2.1% 2,321.4 50.8 60%

Findings: The silhouette method gives its highest score at k = 2, but with k = 2 the split is very coarse (roughly “big” vs “small” firms). I used k = 3 because the silhouette is still reasonable and the third cluster separates out a small group of very large firms, which is more useful for risk screening. The table and chart show that cluster 2 is the high-risk group: it has 830 firms (about 15% of the training data) but a controversy rate of 8.0%, which is about 2.8 times the overall rate (2.8%).

These are the largest firms (median market capitalisation about USD 9,455 million) with the highest environmental scores and the highest share of climate policies. The other clusters sit near or below the average.

This agrees with the Wilcoxon and policy results: large, well-disclosing firms attract the most controversy. Because the clusters were built without the outcome, this link is genuine information that the supervised models can also use.

6.5 Resampling plan and metrics

I use 5-fold cross-validation stratified by the outcome on the training set. The training firms are split into five groups; each model is trained on four groups and scored on the fifth, and this is repeated five times. Every candidate model and every tuning value is therefore scored on data it was not trained on, which protects against overfitting. The pre-processing is re-learned inside each fold, so the validation fold never influences the medians or scaling.

I tune on ROC AUC and also record PR AUC (computed as average precision). The helper functions below build the folds, the metrics and the cross-validation loop.

##        
## fold_id  Yes   No
##       1   31 1061
##       2   31 1061
##       3   31 1060
##       4   31 1060
##       5   30 1060

6.6 Models

I build five candidate models, all using the same cross-validation folds so that the comparison is fair.

1. Logistic regression: Linear model of the log-odds; easy to interpret (odds ratios). I judge it by AUC and choose a low threshold later.

2. Logistic regression + PCA: Same, but on principal components to remove multicollinearity. I tune the number of components.

3. Elastic-net logistic regression: Logistic regression with a penalty that shrinks unimportant coefficients towards zero (a mix of ridge and lasso), which helps when there are many correlated predictors. I tune the penalty and the ridge/lasso mixture (alpha).

4. Decision tree: Rules of the form “if X > a then …”; easy to explain to managers. I give both classes equal prior weight (prior = c(0.5, 0.5)), so the tree does not ignore the rare class.

5. K-nearest neighbours (KNN): Predicts from the most similar firms | I tune the number of neighbours.

The model functions are in the chunk above (fit_logit, fit_logit_pca, fit_enet, fit_tree, fit_knn). Each one fits on a training set and returns the predicted probability of a controversy for new firms.

## $KNN
## # A tibble: 1 × 5
##       k mean_roc_auc se_roc_auc mean_pr_auc se_pr_auc
##   <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl>
## 1    41        0.654     0.0126       0.146    0.0197

Findings: The tuning plots show how performance changes with the settings. For KNN, very small k gives noisy predictions (high variance) and larger k smooths the predictions, which improves AUC until it flattens. For the PCA model, too few components throw away useful information, while more components approach the plain logistic model. For the elastic net, too much penalty shrinks every coefficient towards zero and too little behaves like the plain logistic regression (many noisy coefficients), so performance peaks in between, and a mixture closer to ridge/lasso is chosen by the cross-validation. For the tree, very deep trees with small leaves can overfit; I choose the setting with the best cross-validated ROC AUC for each model.

6.7 Comparing the models using cross-validation

Cross-validated performance (5 folds, training data)
model mean_roc_auc se_roc_auc mean_pr_auc se_pr_auc
Elastic-net logistic regression 0.707 0.008 0.155 0.017
Logistic regression 0.693 0.016 0.134 0.024
Logistic regression + PCA 0.689 0.017 0.127 0.020
KNN 0.654 0.013 0.146 0.020
Decision tree 0.647 0.015 0.072 0.003

Findings: The best model in cross-validation is Elastic-net logistic regression with a ROC AUC of about 0.707. An AUC of 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect, so my values of roughly 0.65 to 0.72 mean the models are better than chance but only modestly, which is consistent with the heavy overlap I saw in the PCA plot. The penalised (elastic-net) logistic regression is ahead, which makes sense because it shrinks the many noisy and correlated coefficients that hurt the plain logistic regression. However, its lead over plain logistic regression, logistic regression with PCA and KNN is small compared with the standard errors, so I should not claim the ranking among these four is certain. The decision tree is clearly the weakest (AUC about 0.65): a single tree is unstable and this data has weak, noisy signals. The PR AUC values are low in absolute terms because only 2.8% of firms are positive (a random model would score about 0.03), so I judge them against that baseline and not against 1; the best models are roughly four to five times better than random on this measure.

6.8 Choosing the decision threshold (using the cost of errors)

A classification model gives a probability, and I must choose a cut-off above which a firm is flagged. The default cut-off of 0.5 is far too high here, because predicted probabilities are small when the event is rare. Since false positives are cheap and false negatives are costly, I choose the cut-off that maximises the F2 score on the out-of-fold training predictions (not on the test set). F2 is the F-score that treats recall as twice as important as precision. I also show some alternative operating points.

Operating points on out-of-fold training predictions
Choice Threshold Sensitivity Specificity Precision Firms flagged
Best F2 (my choice) 0.053 39% 92% 12.9% 9%
Recall at least 60% 0.028 61% 72% 5.9% 29%
Recall at least 70% 0.024 70% 64% 5.3% 37%
Recall at least 80% 0.017 81% 35% 3.5% 66%
Recall at least 90% 0.014 90% 20% 3.2% 80%

Findings: The plot shows the classic trade-off: lowering the threshold catches more controversial firms (higher sensitivity) but flags many more firms (lower precision and specificity). The table translates this into workload. For example, to catch a given share of risky firms the experts must review the percentage of firms shown in the “Firms flagged” column. Because the model is only moderately accurate, catching most risky firms needs a very low threshold and a large review workload (catching about 80% of risky firms means reviewing more than half of all firms). I use the best-F2 threshold as my default recommendation because it reflects the stated cost structure (missing a risky firm is worse than reviewing a safe one) while keeping the review list short. If the experts have more capacity, the manager can pick a lower threshold from the table; if capacity is tight, a higher one.

6.9 Final evaluation on the test set

Now I refit the best model on the whole training set, predict on the test set (the first time it is used), and apply the threshold I chose in 4.8. This gives an honest estimate of how the model would work on new firms.

Test-set AUC for the final model: Elastic-net logistic regression
metric estimate
roc_auc 0.681
pr_auc 0.182
Test-set performance: my threshold vs the default 0.5 cut-off
metric My threshold Default 0.5
sens 0.423 0.019
spec 0.932 1.000
precision 0.155 1.000
accuracy 0.918 0.972
bal_accuracy 0.678 0.510
f2 0.314 0.024

Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on the test set (500 resamples)
metric estimate lower_95 upper_95
ROC AUC 0.681 0.590 0.775
Sensitivity 0.423 0.289 0.557

Findings of the test results:

  • The final model is Elastic-net logistic regression. On the unseen test set its ROC AUC is 0.681, compared with a cross-validated value of about 0.707. The two are close, so I do not see strong signs of overfitting, but the test set has few positives, so I still treat the number as approximate.

  • With my threshold of 0.053, the model catches 42% of the 52 controversial firms in the test set (sensitivity), with a specificity of 93%. The confusion matrix shows 22 true positives, 120 false positives and 30 missed firms (false negatives).

  • Precision is only 15%, meaning most flagged firms are not controversial. In this task that is acceptable (the scenario says false positives are low cost) but experts should know that most flagged firms will be false alarms. Still, this precision is several times higher than the 2.8% base rate, which shows the model concentrates risk.

  • Accuracy looks worse (92%) than for the default 0.5 rule (97%), but that is misleading: the default rule is accurate only because it almost never flags a firm. Its sensitivity is just 2%, so it would miss nearly every risky firm. This is the accuracy paradox for imbalanced data.

  • The gain curve shows how much better than random the ranking is: the further the curve is above the diagonal, the more controversial firms are found early when experts review firms in order of predicted risk.

  • The bootstrap confidence intervals are wide because the test set contains only about 52 positives. I should therefore present performance as a range (for example AUC between about 0.59 and 0.78) and not as a precise number.

6.10 What drives the predictions? (model interpretation)

I fit the logistic regression and the decision tree on the training data to see which variables matter. These two models are the easiest to explain to a non-technical manager.

6.10.1 Logistic regression: odds ratios

The continuous variables are standardised, so each odds ratio shows how the odds of a controversy change when the variable increases by one standard deviation (of its transformed version). A value above 1 means higher risk; below 1 means lower risk. The confidence intervals here are Wald intervals (estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors).

Ten most significant terms in the logistic regression
term odds_ratio conf.low conf.high p.value
fin_cor 0.731 0.614 0.871 0.000
fin_rev 1.384 1.150 1.665 0.001
fin_capex 2.438 1.313 4.529 0.005
env_co2s2 0.689 0.529 0.898 0.006
env_co2s3 1.329 1.078 1.638 0.008
hq_China 0.265 0.092 0.764 0.014
na_ind_env_co2s2 0.239 0.074 0.775 0.017
na_ind_env_co2s1 3.429 1.128 10.424 0.030
capex_intensity 0.693 0.494 0.971 0.033
na_ind_env_energy 1.827 1.033 3.231 0.038

Findings: In my output the most significant terms are size, cost and emission variables (for example revenue, cost of revenue and Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions), together with a few industries. Some size and cost variables have odds ratios above 1 and some below 1, which looks contradictory: for example revenue appears to raise the odds while cost of revenue and Scope 2 emissions appear to lower them. This is the multicollinearity problem I saw in the correlation plot: these variables move together, so the model uses differences between them, and their individual coefficients are unstable and should not be read one by one. I read them together as “size and emissions matter”, and I use the confidence intervals to see how certain each effect is (if the interval crosses 1, the effect is not statistically clear). Industries such as real estate (REITs) and electric utilities have much lower odds than the reference industry, which fits the exploratory result that resource-heavy sectors are riskier than service or property sectors. Industry dummies are compared with the first (alphabetical) industry, which is the baseline.

6.10.2 Decision tree: rules and variable importance

Findings: the tree shows simple “if-then” rules. For readability I draw a simplified three-level tree: the first split is the variable that best separates controversial from non-controversial firms, and boxes with a high share of “Yes” are the high-risk segments that experts should look at first. The variable importance chart comes from the full tuned tree. In my run the most important variables are the size and cost variables (capital expenditure, revenue, cost of revenue and market capitalisation), which agrees with the logistic regression and the clustering result: size drives most of the predictable risk. A single tree is easy to explain, but it is less stable and less accurate than the other models here, so I use it for explanation and not as the final predictor.

6.11 Conclusions and recommendations

  1. Best model: Elastic-net logistic regression gave the best cross-validated ROC AUC (about 0.71) and a test AUC of about 0.68. This is better than chance but only modest, because controversial firms and others overlap heavily on the available data; the bootstrap interval for the test AUC is wide.

  2. How to use it: use the model as a ranking and screening tool. With the chosen threshold it flags about 8% of firms for expert review and catches about 42% of the controversial firms in the test set. Experts can instead review firms from the top of the probability ranking until their capacity runs out (see the gain curve).

  3. Key drivers: firm size and emissions carry the most predictive information (also visible in the clusters and the tree), and industry (especially oil and gas) and country add context in the exploratory analysis. Firms with many policies are not safer: they are often larger and more visible, so having a policy should not be treated as a guarantee.

  4. Why the threshold matters: because false positives are cheap, I lowered the threshold far below 0.5. The default 0.5 would give impressive accuracy but would miss almost all risky firms.

  5. Limitations:

    • Only about 200 of the 7,275 firms have a controversy, so estimates are uncertain (see the bootstrap intervals).

    • env_contro is based on news data, so it measures media-visible controversies, which are biased towards large firms in well-covered countries.

    • Many predictors have missing values, which I handled with median imputation and missing-value indicators.

    • The model finds associations, not causes, and it should not be used to blame firms without expert review.

7 Overall conclusions:

1. Most common climate hazards: Extreme heat, urban flooding and drought are the most reported hazards; by family, flooding / heavy rain, heat and drought / water scarcity affect the most communities. Cities typically face about five hazards at once.

2. Planned projects and funding by region: Project counts are spread across regions, but money is concentrated (UKWW dominates). Three impossible cost values were removed.

3. Ranked investment opportunities: 31 waste-management projects from cities with confirmed business collaboration and loan / PPP funding models, ranked by investment cost.

4. Environmental controversy model: A cross-validated, threshold-tuned screening model with moderate discriminating power; best used to prioritise firms for expert review.
